Adaptively densify lines for a projection

Source: R/densify.R
densify.Rd

Insert vertices along great circle arcs exactly where a target projection bends them, so that straight chords drawn between output vertices stay within tolerance of the true projected curve. This is the adaptive resampling scheme of d3-geo (Bostock), generalized to paths and to segment meshes.

Usage

densify(
  x,
  target,
  source = NULL,
  tolerance = NULL,
  pixels = 2048L,
  max_depth = 16L,
  ellipsoid = FALSE
)

Arguments

x

a two-column matrix of lon,lat (a path), a list of such matrices, a segment mesh (a list with vb, a 4 x n vertex matrix with rows x, y, z, h, and is, a 2 x m segment index matrix, 1-based, as used by rgl's mesh3d), or a wkpool vertex-pool topology from the wkpool package (any wk-handleable geometry via wkpool::establish_topology()); pools carrying z or m vertex values are refused, as densification cannot invent them at new vertices

target

projection for which to densify (proj string, WKT, authority code - anything PROJ accepts)

source

coordinate system of the input. If NULL (the default) it is taken from a wkpool input's own crs when it has one, and otherwise is 'EPSG:4326' (longitude, latitude); authority codes are axis-normalized so 'EPSG:4326' input is still given as lon,lat

tolerance

maximum allowed deviation, in units of target (usually metres); if NULL (the default) it is derived from the larger side of the projected extent of the input as max(diff(range))/pixels

pixels

notional output width/height used to derive the default tolerance, i.e. "keep error under about one part in pixels of the plot"; ignored when tolerance is supplied

max_depth

maximum bisection depth per input segment (each level at most doubles the vertex count of a segment)

ellipsoid

if TRUE, new vertices are placed on the WGS84 geodesic instead of the great circle, using the 'geographiclib' package (which must be installed). The sphere still decides how many vertices each edge gets and at what fraction along it; each one is then moved to the same fraction of the geodesic between the same two endpoints. Input vertices are unchanged, shared edges still get identical vertices, and the input must be longitude, latitude. On long edges the two differ by tens of kilometres (about 23 km at most from Hobart to London)

Value

the same kind of object as x, with vertices added: a matrix for a path, a list of matrices for a list, a mesh with appended vertices and refined is for a mesh, a wkpool with appended vertices (freshly minted .vx ids), refined directed segments, and .feature provenance carried onto every refined segment

Details

The error metric is evaluated in the plane of the target projection: the great circle midpoint of each candidate segment is forward-projected and compared to the segment's planar chord (perpendicular distance, plus a parametric check that catches strong shear). Segments are split recursively until they pass or max_depth is reached. No inverse transforms are used and each point is projected exactly once.

Coordinates are returned in the coordinates of source (geographic by default): project the result yourself for plotting, e.g. with rproj_xy() for a matrix or, for wk geometry (such as wkpool::segments_to_wkb() of a refined pool), with wk::wk_transform() and a PROJ::proj_trans_create() transform.

Points that cannot be projected (for example beyond the horizon of an orthographic projection) do not error: segments touching them are left un-densified, and refinement stops at unprojectable midpoints. Clipping is out of scope here.

Inserted vertices are emitted in the longitude frame of their input edge: an edge along longitude 180 refines at 180, its mirror at -180 refines at -180 (the two seams of a global layer remain distinct), and an edge written as crossing the antimeridian yields a locally continuous chain, possibly outside [-180, 180). Input vertices are always returned with their written values, so a crossing edge's path carries one numeric 360-degree step at its far endpoint (the same point on the sphere; PROJ is indifferent). Longitudes are never canonicalized; normalize afterwards if a canonical range is needed. Edges that cross the target projection's own discontinuity (which depends on lon_0) cannot form a valid planar chain and should be cut beforehand; refinement of such edges is bounded, not exploded, because arcs spanning less ground than tolerance are never split.

Every edge is a great circle arc on a sphere, the same reading of an edge that 's2' uses. Data whose edges are meant as straight lines in longitude and latitude describe a different shape, and densifying them here changes it.

Shared edges stay shared. An edge refines to the same vertices whichever way it is written, bit for bit, so two neighbouring polygons get identical new vertices along their common boundary (and wkpool::merge_coincident() fuses them). An edge that appears twice with the same vertices, as in a merged pool or a segment mesh, is refined once and its new vertices are reused.

References

https://bost.ocks.org/mike/example/

Examples

s <- segment(c(140, -164), c(-89, 80))
d <- densify(s, "+proj=laea +lon_0=147 +lat_0=-42")
nrow(d)
#> [1] 38
plot(rproj_xy(d, "+proj=laea +lon_0=147 +lat_0=-42"), type = "l", asp = 1)

## on the WGS84 ellipsoid rather than the sphere
if (requireNamespace("geographiclib", quietly = TRUE)) {
  e <- densify(d[c(1, nrow(d)), ], "+proj=laea +lon_0=147 +lat_0=-42",
               ellipsoid = TRUE)
  lines(rproj_xy(e, "+proj=laea +lon_0=147 +lat_0=-42"), col = "firebrick")
}
